newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mark higher on European crosses after French vote.
newsitem.headline: Mark higher on European crosses after French vote.

text.p: The mark rose against several European currencies after initial projections showed the opposition left fared better than expected in the first round of voting for the May 25-June 1 French parliamentary election.

Traders and analysts said if the opposition Socialists were to win in the second round of voting on June 1, doubts about the smooth passage towards European Economic and Monetary Union could support German assets against other European markets.

The Italian lira dropped to 987.55/85 against the mark from 984.50/70 just prior to the first result predictions released at 1800 GMT. The franc was slightly weaker against the mark but traders said it would probably be supported by Bank of France intervention.

The result "could be negative for the lira and the peseta as well...seen as negative for convergence trades if the Socialists got a victory," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance said. "Although at the end of the campaign they were a bit softer on Europe, they sounded if they were coming back to a more centrist line."
Traders in Paris said although most desks were manned in France the demand for the mark was coming from non-resident institutions trading in New York.
"There's not too much activity but all the mark crosses are in demand and the dollar is down. Everything mark is in demand," said a trader at a French bank in Paris.
"The result was a surprise and is worring many foreigners. The Parisians are there but the big orders are coming out of New York," he said.
He said the lira would find some support at 989 against the mark and the franc, trading at 3.3744 compared with 3.3714 before the result, could be held at 3.3750.

Analysts said the risk facing European markets was that the conditions the Socialists have attached to France joining a single currency could spark opposition from Germany and possibly cause a delay to the project or derail it.

"I think other European markets will suffer as people worry about EMU uncertainties," Nomura economist Sonja Gibbs said. "True, the Socialists have been making all the right sounds for EMU, saying yes we are for EMU, but the conditions they are attaching to France's participation in EMU are really onerous."

Traders said the knee-jerk reaction to the first election indications in the foreign exchange markets was to buy the mark on the view the German unit would be a stronger currency if on its own than as part of a single currency.
The dollar was trading at 1.6865/70 against the mark at 2006 GMT, down from 1.6925 before the first French election predictions were released at 1800 GMT.

The Socialist party set four conditions for joining a single currency -- including a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty with Italy and Spain joining from the start, a European "economic government", a euro which is not overvalued against the dollar and a new solidarity and growth pact to help tackle unemployment.

Analysts said, however, the Socialists conditions are not that different from those of the ruling centre-right RPR-UDF coalition and stressed that both mainstream parties share a common French vision of Europe, where strong political input would balance the power of the future European central bank.
Many believe a Socialist government would compromise on European issues with France's other partners in the European Union, just as the centre-right did, to make a single currency possible.
